summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Ethernet, and how link-local and autoconfigured addresses are formed there. It also defines the link-layer address option for neighbor discovery messages. It is a proposed standard and replaces RFC 1972.

eli5.summary: This explains how to put IPv6 packets into the standard Ethernet frames that go over network cables, and how a device makes its address there.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets ride inside Ethernet frames, and how an Ethernet card gets its IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs agreed rules for being carried on Ethernet: what the frame looks like, how big packets can be, and how a node builds its addresses and finds its neighbors there.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets go in standard Ethernet frames with type code 86DD hexadecimal. The interface identifier comes from the card's 48-bit address via EUI-64, and IPv6 multicast addresses map to Ethernet addresses starting with 3333.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2464 replaced RFC 1972. It is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6085 and RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2464 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1972. It has been updated by RFC 6085 and RFC 8064, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: What This RFC Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2464 specifies three things for IPv6 on Ethernet: the frame format, the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses, and the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option.

That option is used in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages when they are sent on an Ethernet. The document replaces RFC 1972, which the text says will become historic.

For this document, the term Ethernet includes CSMA/CD and full-duplex subnetworks based on ISO/IEC 8802-3, with various data rates.
sections.eli5: It is a short instruction sheet for using IPv6 on ordinary network cables: how to pack the data, how to name your device, and how to find your neighbors.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
The default MTU for IPv6 packets on an Ethernet is 1500 octets. That size may be reduced by a Router Advertisement carrying an MTU option with a smaller value, or by manual configuration of each node.

If a Router Advertisement on an Ethernet interface carries an MTU option larger than 1500, or larger than a manually configured value, the option may be logged to system management but must otherwise be ignored. Information received from DHCP counts as manually configured.
sections.eli5: A truck can only carry so much at once. The default load is 1500 bytes, and a router can ask you to carry less, but never more.

sections.title: The Ethernet Frame
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are sent in standard Ethernet frames. The Ethernet header holds the destination and source Ethernet addresses and the Ethernet type code, which must contain the value 86DD hexadecimal.

The data field holds the IPv6 header followed immediately by the payload, and possibly padding octets to reach the minimum frame size for the Ethernet link.
sections.eli5: The frame is an envelope with the receiver's address, your address, and a stamp that says 'IPv6 inside'. The letter goes in the middle.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The Interface Identifier of an Ethernet interface is based on the EUI-64 identifier derived from the interface's built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address. The first three octets (the OUI) become the company_id of the EUI-64, the fourth and fifth octets are set to FFFE hexadecimal, and the last three octets of the Ethernet address become the last three octets of the EUI-64.

The Interface Identifier is then made by complementing the Universal/Local bit, the next-to-lowest order bit of the first octet. For the built-in address 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE the result is 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE.

A different MAC address set manually or by software should not be used for this. An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of an Ethernet interface must be 64 bits long. The link-local address is formed by appending the Interface Identifier to the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.eli5: Your device builds its name from the serial number printed on its network card, with a little flip of one switch. Then it adds a standard 'this street only' start to make an address for talking to neighbors.

sections.title: Mapping IPv6 Addresses to Ethernet Addresses
sections.content:
For unicast addresses, the mapping procedure is described in the Neighbor Discovery specification. This RFC defines the Source/Target Link-layer Address option for Ethernet: a Type field (1 for a Source Link-layer address, 2 for a Target Link-layer address), a Length of 1 in units of 8 octets, and the 48-bit Ethernet address in canonical bit order.

That address is the one the interface currently responds to, which may differ from the built-in address used to derive the Interface Identifier.

For multicast, a packet with destination address DST (octets DST[1] to DST[16]) is sent to the Ethernet multicast address whose first two octets are 3333 hexadecimal and whose last four octets are DST[13] through DST[16].
sections.eli5: To mail a neighbor you need their street number on the cable. For group messages, the last part of the group address is copied behind a fixed beginning, like writing a group name on a shared mailbox.

sections.title: Differences From RFC 1972
sections.content:
The Address Token, which was a node's 48-bit MAC address, is replaced by the Interface Identifier, which is 64 bits long and based on the EUI-64 format. An IEEE-defined mapping exists from 48-bit MAC addresses to EUI-64 form.

A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration must now be 64 bits long rather than 80, and the link-local prefix is also shortened to 64 bits.
sections.eli5: The old rule used a shorter name tag and a longer street. The new rule uses a longer name tag and a shorter street, so the two always add up the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The way Interface Identifiers are derived from MAC addresses is meant to preserve global uniqueness when possible. The RFC adds that there is no protection from duplication through accident or forgery.
sections.eli5: Your name tag comes from a serial number that should be one of a kind. But nobody stops two devices from wearing the same tag by mistake or on purpose.
